what: A check on the sparse corrections that needs no reference decoder, because agreeing with Dolby cannot tell `oadec is right` from `oadec repeats Dolby's mistake`
the_idea: an object's level is continuous across a frame boundary unless the content changes, and a matrix that is wrong for one frame makes it jump. So decode the same clip twice, once under each reading, and compare the size of the step at the boundaries of the sparse frames with the step at every other boundary of the same decode. The other boundaries are the control and they are identical between the two decodes, because the reading only touches sparse frames
method: root-mean-square level over 256 samples either side of each frame boundary, in decibels, median over the objects. Sparse boundaries are both edges of a sparse frame

the_settled_clip.material: Extraction 2, 500 frames from 197 000: 58 sparse frames, 870 sparse objects
the_settled_clip.reading: under the reading in use the sparse boundaries are slightly quieter than the ordinary ones -- 1,54 against 1,81 -- which is what a correct matrix looks like. Under the printed reading they are noisier, and the worst of them is nearly twice as big

and_they_all_point_the_same_way: four clips, and in every one the reading in use leaves a smaller step at the sparse boundaries than the printed reading does. Red Notice is the clearest at 2,60 against 4,59
how_much_this_is_worth: much less than the differential, and it answers a question the differential cannot. The 50 dB the sparse corrections are worth against Dolby is a far stronger measurement of *whether the correction is right in detail*; what it cannot rule out is that both decoders share a mistake. A continuity signal comes from the audio rather than from another decoder, and it agrees. It is small -- a fifth of a decibel in the median -- because most objects at a sparse boundary are not badly affected either way; the worst case is the clearer half of it
